item.title: Why You Can’t Just “Be Happy” For Them
item.description:
Jealousy

Why You Can’t Just “Be Happy” For Them

The two emotions hiding inside envy, and how to work with each one.

Posted July 29, 2026

Key points
  • Envy isn't one emotion. It's desire plus disappointment.
  • When you feel envious, run a "desire double-check" first: you may be craving something you don't even want.
  • When desire is real but unattainable, fully feeling the disappointment is what softens envy.

“My best friend was promoted again,” he muttered, halfway through our conversation about something else.

In therapy, it’s the detours that often take us to the main point.

For over a year, Jonah had been trying to advance at his company. “It’s even more annoying because he told me he didn’t really care about the new job. It’s getting harder to pick up his calls. I know I shouldn’t feel this way. Why can’t I just be happy for him?”

“Is it true you’re not happy for him?” I pressed. “Perhaps you are happy, but your envy overshadows your happiness.”

“I don’t know. I’ve tried to practice gratitude; focus on the positive. But that didn’t work. Now I feel worse because I realize I’m both envious and ungrateful. If there’s any part of me that’s happy for him underneath all this, I can’t find it.”

“There might be a way forward,” I replied, “but I’m not sure gratitude’s the right path. Maybe we should start by looking at envy’s parts.”

He gave me a look like I misunderstood him. “That’s what I’ve been trying to do. But until I get myself promoted, I don’t think I can shake this one feeling.”

But envy isn’t one emotion. It’s two.

Understanding Envy: Two Emotions, Three Responses

Envy is challenging partly because it hides two emotions within it. The first is desire. I don’t mean the desire to become another person. It’s desire for some quality, possession, or circumstance we perceive as valuable, even if we dislike the person who has it. When we envy, we see something we wish to possess or emulate. If desire were missing, we wouldn’t be drawn towards the object of envy in the first place. Whether it’s a new car, someone’s talent, or their physical beauty, envy contains the pull of desire.

The second feeling inside of envy is the feeling of disappointment: the reaction to not having this special something, the recognition that what another holds is missing in our own lives. Neuroimaging research by Takahashi and colleagues found that envy activates the same region of the brain tied to the distress of physical pain, and so this disappointment is more like a deep ache. But with my clients, we talk about envy as the combination of desire and disappointment.

When the two emotions inside envy are made clear, three paths to address them emerge.

  1. Run a desire double-check. The first thing we can do is evaluate what we desire. Do I actually want what I envy? Or have I started craving something I don't really want? Perhaps I wanted something because someone else wanted it, what the theorist René Girard called mimetic desire; it’s borrowed rather than truly our own. I may have been charmed by an expensive home, but when I examine this desire more carefully, it turns out to be thinner than I thought. If my desire doesn't survive this double-check, one of envy's underlying feelings falls away, and so the envy fades with it.
  2. Move closer to what’s attainable. When our desire survives the double-check, the next step is to ask if what’s wanted is realistically attainable. It might be possible to close the distance on our disappointment. I may not be able to afford my friend’s vacation, but perhaps I can move towards rest and play in my own life. And when I move closer to what I want, my disappointment softens, and so does the envy.
  3. Fully experience the disappointment. But what about when we continue to want the unattainable? What can be done when desire remains, but the disappointment does, too? When we envy another’s enduring marriage or a sibling’s inheritance? These are the most challenging cases, but in these moments, we must thoroughly experience the disappointment.

Disappointment will knock at the door until we open it. Once we turn the handle and allow it in, many disappointments will depart; they don’t intend to move in permanently but only ask for a hard conversation. Others will stay, but in time, they move to the far end of the house. Late at night, we might bump into them in the hallway, but eventually they leave the main floor. This makes room for other, more pleasant emotions to draw nearer in our everyday lives.

Experiencing disappointment is useful because it carries motion within it, but only as potential, locked until the feeling is felt all the way through. Once fully felt, it moves: disappointment’s wheels begin to turn, the feeling softens or departs, and the envy resting upon it softens too.

Source: Saja Fi / Unsplash

Back to Jonah: Understanding Leads to Action

When Jonah ran his own desire double-check, he discovered that the promotion represented something important to him. It was a symbol of recognition for all the hard work he’d put in. This double-check didn’t change what he wanted, but it clarified why he wanted it.

The second question took more time. With that new understanding, Jonah began asking how to close the distance on his disappointment. He realized that he’d never shared this hope for recognition with his supervisor, because he hadn’t understood it in himself until now. He had new steps he could take.

What remained couldn’t be reasoned away. The disappointment that this promotion wasn’t happening on his timeline didn’t leave, but after he felt it all the way through, it began to ease. And as it did, his friendship became comfortable again.

--

Envy can feel impossible to overcome when it’s treated as a single emotion. But when our desires and disappointments are made clear, each feeling can be addressed independently: we can run a desire double-check, move closer to what's attainable, or fully experiencing the disappointment underneath. It’s when we address envy’s hidden parts that we become less captured by the lives of others, and more fulfilled within our own.

"Jonah" is a composite character. His story draws on patterns I've observed across many clients I've worked with; no identifying details from any individual client are included.

item.title: Why Are Rats, Mice, and Birds Excluded from Animalhood?
item.description:
Animal Behavior

Why Are Rats, Mice, and Birds Excluded from Animalhood?

As absurd as this sounds, a major animal welfare act claims they're not animals.

Posted July 29, 2026

Key points
  • Those who ignore ample data about animal minds wrongly criticize the use of anecdotes and anthropomorphism.
  • Scientific uncertainty and mistaken claims about human exceptionalism also result in intentional data-denying.
  • Data deniers take the easy way out by misrepresenting detailed research that results in mistreatment.
Rats form close friendships.
Source: Brendan Christopher/Pexels.

A question that I'm repeatedly asked: "Why is there a lag between learning facts about animal consciousness, sentience, and emotions and using what we know?" Mary, a well-known psychologist who calls herself a cognitive ethologist—someone who studies animal minds—wrote me a nice note asking me to say more, if I could, about the mindset of people who feel comfortable denying scientific facts about animal minds while continuing to do harmful research that has little to no bearing on who the animals really are.

Why animals "lose their minds" and the downsides of data-denying

One of the most egregious and surprising examples of animals losing their minds due to ignoring detailed comparative data on animal cognition and emotions for these clearly sentient and deeply emotional beings can be found in the current updated US Federal Animal Welfare Act, where we read,

"Enacted January 23, 2002, Title X, Subtitle D of the Farm Security and Rural Investment Act, changed the definition of 'animal' in the Animal Welfare Act, specifically excluding birds, rats of the genus Rattus, and mice of the genus Mus, bred for use in research."

I am always incredulous that the Animal Welfare Act does not consider these indisputable animals to be animals. Of course, these rodents are the go-to animals used by the millions in various invasive studies; this use must be defended. Other indisputable animals also are conveniently tossed out of the animal kingdom. People are shocked when I tell them this. We know from detailed scientific research that they have highly evolved cognitive and emotional capacities, they experience empathy, and rats laugh and like to be tickled. We know that tickling laboratory rats is good for science. What more do we need to show that these are sentient beings with rich and deep emotional lives?

Why is data denied?

This question is covered in great detail in two books with numerous references to scientific research.1 Here is a summary of these lengthy discussions; most people do not know why some researchers ignore a wealth of scientific research.1 In addition to the popularity of paradigm science, economic incentives, and laws and regulations that are built on faulty assumptions and misreadings of available data, I highlight four reasons why this occurs.

Scientific uncertainty means that an ever-declining number of skeptics claim that existing data do not prove other animals are richly and deeply emotional, sometimes saying that we don't even know if they are conscious or sentient. While a dwindling number of people still claim we can never know precisely what a nonhuman animal (animal) is truly feeling, most researchers and the vast majority of lay people do not doubt that these and many animals are highly sentient beings.

Anecdotes are all you offer. This claim is false; animal consciousness studies use real, hard data, not fabricated stories. Thus, animals are only acting "as if" they have feelings when they really don't. Nothing could be further from scientific truth.2

Oh, you're just being anthropomorphic by claiming animals are feeling beings. This is one of the most common criticisms by deniers. Anthropomorphism is unavoidable and is extremely useful when used carefully, critically, and biocentrically precisely because humans have no other vocabulary for describing the subjective experiences of nonhuman animals. Anthropomorphism makes animals' worlds accessible to us, but it does not mean animals feel exactly what we feel, or even what other individuals of the same or other species feel. Anthropomorphic language functions as a bridge for understanding rather than a literal scientific claim of identity between human and animal experience. Mindful anthropomorphism works.

Anthropomorphic language also helps us better understand other animals and highlights their individual personalities, and it's not "more anthropomorphic" to say an animal is unhappy than to say they're happy. It's time to accept the benefits of anthropomorphism and use it on behalf of other animals. Naysayers about the usefulness of "being anthropomorphic" and those who ignore what we now know and have known for many decades about animal minds and hearts need to get over it and appreciate the benefits of recognizing it. Eminent researcher Frans de Waal argues that anthropodenial no longer works—the "blindness to the humanlike characteristics of other animals or the animal-like characteristics of ourselves."

This apt quotation is right on the mark:

The mental territory we can claim to be 'uniquely human' is shrinking at an alarming rate. Wasps can distinguish faces, dolphins call one another by name, pigs use tools, zebra finches dream, parrots go on Zoom, and sometimes crayfish get anxious. Chimps, meanwhile, exist in complex cultures, rather like ours, with fashion trends.–Martha Gill3

Anthropocentrism argues for human exceptionalism and refers to false claims that humans are exceptional or superior beings— "better," "more valuable," or "higher" than nonhumans—or smarter, more sentient, and experience deeper emotional lives. Thus, claims about what other animals feel, whether supported by science or not, don't change the fact that they are separate and below and inferior to humans on some purported human-created scale of complexity. Clearly, they are not less than us.4

Follow the science: Animal minds are dynamic, rich, and deep

Studying animal minds and learning what's in them and how they work can range from being fairly easy to being incredibly difficult. There is wide-ranging and ever-growing interest in animal minds, and ample research clearly shows that denying animals the emotional capacities they clearly possess is highly unscientific. Why aren't myriad scientists who know that rats, mice, birds and other animals are indeed minded animals speaking out against this?

Rather than playing a role in animals losing their minds, we should celebrate and respect them for who they are and not worry about whether this means we are "lesser mammals." We're not. Frans de Waal wonders if we're not smart enough to know what's happening in animal minds.

We are not the standard or measure against whom other animals should be measured. We are a highly variable and exceptional species just like countless other animals. Changing our ways and valuing other animals will be better for them and for us, and this is precisely where current science takes us.

item.title: Knowledge Is Not Always Power When It Concerns the Future
item.description:
Dementia

Knowledge Is Not Always Power When It Concerns the Future

Balancing the cost/benefit of learning today about your brain tomorrow.

Posted July 29, 2026

Key points
  • Knowing Alzheimer's risk may cause years of anxiety without guaranteeing illness will occur.
  • Predictive Alzheimer’s tests show only increased risk, not certainty of developing the disease.
  • Current laws don’t fully protect predictive test results from insurers or other third parties.

If you had the opportunity to learn with near-perfect certainty from a blood test whether or not you are destined to become afflicted with Alzheimer’s disease or some other currently incurable brain disease, would you take it?

Let’s assume that you would prefer to learn the results of the test. At what age would you prefer to learn your fate? “Probably toward the last decade or so of my life,” you might say, “but not in my twenties or thirties.” That’s the choice of most people I’ve asked. At whatever age, what would you do with that knowledge?

While pondering that question, let’s explore some of the implications if you decide not to take the test: First, before making your decision, you should know that treatments for Alzheimer’s disease leave much to be desired. Anti-amyloid therapies slow the progression of the disease by only 6 to 9 months.

What’s more, the treatments themselves carry the risk of life-threatening brain swelling, which requires urgent critical care, perhaps even brain surgery. In addition, a review issued in 2026, which analyzed 17 anti-amyloid studies with a total of 20,342 patients, concluded that the effect on amyloid dementia was “trivial” and the effect on functional ability was described as “small at best,” according to the researchers.

And there are other factors that must be taken into account. Thirty percent of elderly people who are perfectly normal cognitively and never develop Alzheimer’s show amyloid deposits in their brains. Further, you should also know that even among a small number of those with Apoe-4, the genotype most associated with advanced Alzheimer’s disease, a small number may show no signs of the disease and lead perfectly normal lives. Conclusion? If you decide to have the test and it turns up positive, it’s possible you’ll spend the last decades of your life fretting about something horrible that isn’t going to take place.

Am I Going to Come Down With Alzheimer's Disease or Not?

Predictions about dire neurological diseases first became possible in the 1970s and 80s with Huntington’s disease, an inherited neurological disorder which can be predicted if the mutation responsible for the disease is positive. Even today, the disease remains incurable, with the loser in this Huntington’s gene lottery destined to an almost certain death marked by chorea (uncontrollable movements), thinking and memory problems, difficulty with speech and swallowing, severely impaired walking with accompanying loss of balance, and impulse control problems (temper outbursts, impulsivity).

While considering these factors, it’s important to emphasize that the test for Alzheimer’s, when positive, implies an increased risk, not by any means a certainty, that the disease will develop (as discussed above).

Assumptions about the initial testing for Huntington’s didn’t go according to expectations: Instead of the majority of people at risk choosing to know their fate—the expectation of both the doctors and geneticists—only 10-20% of people at risk chose to proceed with genetic testing. Based on this unexpected and startling finding, the future of genetic testing was forever changed. As a cornerstone of current genetic counseling, not only do people at risk have a “right to know,” but those who decide against testing also have a right to choose “not to know.”

So let’s assume at this point you’ve made your choice. You’re probably wondering how it compares with national findings of a US survey of adults aged 65 and older. It found that 75% responded that they would “take a free definitively predictive Alzheimer test, leaving only 25% stating that they would not”.

While the reasons for seeking testing are fairly straightforward (ranging from researching custodial care options, deciding on advanced directions, such as whether or not to be resuscitated, and financial planning), the reasons for not knowing are more focused on internal rather than external features: freedom from living under a cloud of doom, staving off anxiety and desperation and, finally, the conviction that uncertainty is easier to live with than certainty.

Surprisingly, it turned out that being told of a higher risk of Alzheimer’s did not necessarily lead to the catastrophic psychological harms that both patients and their doctors feared. This was yet another indicator of the uncertainty regarding people’s willingness to enter into what some consider a kind of Faustian bargain.

Loss of Medical Autonomy

Whether or not you choose to learn about your Alzheimer's fate, you’re likely to favor limiting the spread of that information to people or institutions of your choosing. Such a personal preference is unlikely to prevail under current medical, cultural, and political circumstances.

Although laws currently on the books, such as The Genetic Information Non-Discrimination Act and The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), offer some level of protection, don’t count on either of them to guarantee that you can maintain control over such sensitive and, to certain players in the health field, financially profitable information. For one thing, the Alzheimer’s prediction tests rely on blood markers, not genetic findings. Further, GINA applies only to health insurance but not disability insurance or long-term care insurance. In most states, your results are fair game for the disability and long-term care bean counters for whom you are nothing but a statistic. If you oppose them in any way, things will turn sour quickly. They’ll either deny you the insurance (the most likely result) or compel your compliance via litigation.

Here are three provisions for medical release and authorization presented recently for signature to a patient of mine seeking long-term care insurance.

One, “I am permitting to be disclosed and used any information on my medical history, and the diagnosis, prognosis and treatment of any physical or mental condition.”

Two, “My health information may be redisclosed [i.e. sent to others] and no longer protected by applicable law, including federal health information privacy regulations.”

Three, “If I do not sign this authorization for my long-term care insurance, my application may not be processed.”

So does this additional information alter your confidence in the decision you made a moment ago about learning your Alzheimer fate?

Are you prepared to accept all of the potential consequences of letting the genie out of a bottle?

Richard M. Restak, M.D.

item.title: Toxic Workplaces, Veiled in Gaslighting, Can Lead to Suicide
item.description:
Gaslighting

Toxic Workplaces, Veiled in Gaslighting, Can Lead to Suicide

Employees should be trained to assess their workplaces for risk.

Posted July 29, 2026

Key points
  • Too many healthcare workplaces allow physicians and other staff to resort to self-harm.
  • Gaslighting responses to this tragic outcome may reinforce employees' belief that their struggle is internal.
  • Gaslighting may lead to a focus on mental illness to deflect from occupational hazards facing employees.

The workplace is treacherous at present. From job loss threatened by AI, to scapegoating truth-tellers, to funds being funnelled to the top of corporations while workers can hardly stay afloat in a cost-of-living crisis, it’s too easy for employees to internalize the stress and the injustice. Workers may believe their suffering is a personal defect, rather than recognizing a systemic failure of modern society that benefits the wealthy and abandons workers.

Drawing on the research of trauma expert Dr. Heliana Ramirez, who studies suicides among healthcare workers, we see that it could be life-saving to assess one’s workplace for potential risk factors that negatively impact mental health. Considering that in America “suicide is the second leading cause of death for medical residents in training,” as Ramirez highlights, being proactive about one's work environment and conditions is a critical safety issue.

When Ramirez notes that suicide for “registered nurses, healthcare support workers, and mental health technicians” is even higher than it is for medical residents and physicians, we realize how necessary it is for employees to be informed and trained to assess dangers to themselves at work.

Ramirez encourages us to reframe extreme work stress and work trauma-related mental “illness” as mental “injury.” Instead of asking what’s wrong with employees, we should ask “how were employees injured at work?” By focusing on the working conditions causing workplace trauma, we identify the source of the injury, which allows us to better protect those at risk.

What to do when the workplace itself is the source of harm

A documentary film led by physicians on the healthcare crisis, Suck it Up, Buttercup, was released this year with a focus on workplace conditions. The documentary does not fault victims. It is laser-focused on occupational hazards: “The U.S. healthcare system is unraveling, burdened by corporate greed, overwhelming bureaucracy, and a work environment that is driving clinicians to exhaustion and patients to harm.”

Ramirez is clear that suicide prevention too often focuses on coping and self-care rather than zoning in on “occupational hazards,” and this is where a gaslighting approach insinuates itself into this extreme crisis. Healthcare employees are misrepresented as failing to utilize employee wellness programs when a suicidal crisis is triggered by moral injury and institutional betrayal. Garrick and Buck (2022) report in “The Psychosocial Impacts of Whistleblower Retaliation” that 50% of whistleblowers who experience retaliation for reporting illegal and unethical behavior in the workplace experience suicidal crisis.

The Suck it Up, Buttercup film removes the gaslighting veil that covers up toxic workplace conditions, and gives voice to those suffering in psychologically unsafe workplaces: “The film lifts the veil on a dangerous dysfunction that has remained hidden for far too long, from unsafe staffing to financial pressures to the moral injury felt by those trying to provide care in a broken system.” When systems are broken at work, it may lead to mental injuries.

Assess whether your workplace has invisible toxins

Imagine a workplace that makes employees ill or leads to their death from asbestos, lead, or carbon monoxide. You can’t see these toxins, but they are dangerous for your health. Would you be safer consulting prevention manuals about coping and self-care? When the source of illness is covered up because it has not been identified, employees’ nervous systems may crash in the freeze trauma response. After attempts to address the problem (i.e., fight) are thwarted and employees are unable to flee the danger of a workplace they sacrificed years of study and exorbitant student loans to afford, they may collapse into suicide. These are the preventable tragedies that drive the physicians’ documentary Suck it Up, Buttercup.

We need our physicians and nurses safe and healthy
Source: Travisdmchenry / Pixabay

What are some workplace dangers that employees might identify as potentially leading to suicidal crisis? Focusing on healthcare, Ramirez lists institutional risk factors that could activate suicidal crisis that workers can use to assess their own safety:

  • hostile patients
  • extreme work hours
  • collegial bullying
  • sleep deprivation
  • inadequate resources
  • licensure reporting requirements
  • understaffing

For women health workers of colour, add these:

  • racial battle fatigue
  • sexism

Ramirez highlights “[p]hysicians’ culture of 'medical exceptionalism, medicalization, and individual responsibility' as sources of burnout. Not only are doctors trained to be 'self-negating,' they are 'stigmatized for disclosing work-related mental injury.'”

Ramirez notes that “systemic racism” is an additional psychosocial workplace hazard facing clinicians of color. Injury from medical culture can be fatal, as exemplified by Dr. Nakita Mortimer, a Haitian-American anesthesiology resident who died by suicide in 2023. Ramirez notes: “Dr. Mortimer’s death epitomizes occupational demoralization syndrome” which is acquired from what the Association of Black Women Physicians calls the “diseased system for which we work.”

How does gaslighting lead to self-blame?

As documented in my bookThe Gaslit Brain, focused specifically on workplace harm, gaslighting’s insidious trick is to fault the one injured, creating an internal belief that they are mentally weak or unstable. Ramirez and the many physicians involved in Suck It Up, Buttercup expose gaslighting and its dangerous deception. In The Gaslit Brain, two employees who became suicidal noted that they did not even know the term “gaslighting,” let alone the way the behaviour was leading them into possible self-harm. They internalized the psycho-social injuries being done to them, and believed they were to blame.

Documentary film Suck it Up, Buttercup asserts that it “is more than a film. It is a movement calling for transparency, accountability, and a future where healthcare works for the people it was built to serve.” Gaslighting is transparency's and accountability’s greatest enemy. Gaslighting pulls the veil over unsafe workplaces and occupational hazards, making employees believe their problems are due to mental illness, when in fact, they could be due to mental injury.

Ramirez explains that “systemic suicide prevention is needed at the micro-employee nervous system and macro-employer healthcare system levels with resources that avoid professional barriers to care, increase a sense of safety in one’s body, and reduce isolation and shame.” The final section of her article details brain-informed and nervous system-informed strategies that employees can apply to stay safe and healthy at work.

If you or someone you love is contemplating suicide, seek help immediately. For help 24/7 dial 988 for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or reach out to the Crisis Text Line by texting TALK to 741741. To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Why Your Inner Battle May Be Keeping You Stuck
item.description:
Emotion Regulation

Why Your Inner Battle May Be Keeping You Stuck

Healing begins when the fight within ourselves ends.

Posted July 29, 2026

Key points
  • Fighting emotional struggles often increases suffering.
  • Healing comes from curiosity and compassion, not combat.
  • Letting go of the battle means listening to distress with compassion, not attacking it.
Source: Free Adobe stock by Andranik123

"When you fight something, you're tied to it forever. As long as you're fighting it, you're giving it power."—Anthony de Mello

Many of us have heard the familiar advice: Keep fighting. Never give up. The adversary may be an illness, a social injustice, a difficult circumstance, or a mental health challenge. We live in a culture that celebrates fighting. We fight wars, diseases, inequalities, and even our own emotions.

Over the years, countless clients have told me they have been "fighting" depression, anxiety, PTSD, or other mental health struggles for most of their lives. Well-meaning friends and loved ones have encouraged them to stay strong and keep fighting, believing perseverance is the path to healing. But what should we make of this deep attachment to the idea of "fighting the good fight"? Who determines what qualifies as a good fight? More importantly, is fighting our emotional and psychological struggles an effective strategy?

My experience, both personal and professional, has led me to a different conclusion: the fight mentality is often misguided, counterproductive, and, paradoxically, a significant source of suffering.

We are often taught that we are hardwired to respond to threats through the fight-or-flight response. Flight is relatively easy to understand—we distance ourselves from what we perceive as threatening. Fight, however, involves moving toward the threat in an attempt to control, overcome, or eliminate it.

The problem is that many people facing depression, anxiety, or trauma already feel exhausted, overwhelmed, helpless, or hopeless. The call to "stay strong" and "keep fighting" can feel impossible. For some, life has delivered so many blows that getting back up for another round seems more daunting than staying down.

Through my own struggles with depression and anxiety, and through years of working with others facing similar challenges, I have come to believe that we often miss the mark when we adopt a battle mindset toward our emotional lives.

The very act of fighting something gives it power. When the struggle is internal, the consequences become even more troubling. You cannot fight depression, anxiety, or fear without, in some sense, fighting the self in which those experiences arise. The result is an internal division—a feeling many people describe as being "at war with myself."

Letting go of the fight mentality does not mean surrendering to suffering or resigning ourselves to a life of emotional pain. Rather, it means we release the need to conquer our inner experiences and approach them with compassionate curiosity. This shift requires less strength than trust—the willingness to believe that our minds and bodies are not working against us. Often, they are attempting to communicate something important. Instead of attacking our distress, we can learn to listen to it.

The poet Rainer Maria Rilke captured this beautifully in a letter to a young poet:

You must think that something is happening with you, that life has not forgotten you, that it holds you in its hand; it will not let you fall. Why do you want to shut out of your life any uneasiness, any miseries, or any depressions? For after all, you do not know what work these conditions are doing inside you.

At this point, many people understandably respond, "That's easier said than done."

They're right.

First, letting go of the fight mentality means challenging habits that have been reinforced both culturally and biologically. We have been taught to battle discomfort, not to befriend it.

Second, many people do not have the energy to continue fighting. Years of struggling with anxiety, depression, grief, or trauma can leave emotional reserves depleted.

Finally, it is never a fair fight. Depression and anxiety are not external enemies. They arise from within the mind itself and know every vulnerability, every fear, and every hiding place. Sadness may disguise itself as anger. Anxiety often manifests physically through tension, restlessness, or illness. Fighting these experiences can become an exhausting cycle that only deepens our distress.

The alternative is not passivity. It is emotional regulation, self-compassion, and acceptance. These approaches are supported by thousands of years of contemplative and spiritual traditions as well as modern research in psychology and neuroscience. From Christian teachings about finding meaning in suffering to the Buddha's focus on understanding suffering and its cessation, wisdom traditions have long suggested that relief comes not from waging war against our pain but from changing our relationship to it.

Healing often begins not when we fight harder, but when we stop treating ourselves as the enemy.
